hook.text: Airflow in a roaster does three jobs at once: transfers heat, removes smoke, and carries away chaff from the beans.

buildup.text: More airflow means more convective heat and faster roasting. Less airflow means more conduction from the drum.

discovery.text: Skilled roasters adjust airflow at different stages—lower during drying, higher during development to push flavors forward.

twist.text: Insufficient airflow traps smoke inside the drum. The beans absorb it, creating a harsh, smoky off-flavor called 'tipping.'

climax.text: Airflow is the most under-discussed variable in roasting. Many flavor problems blamed on temperature are actually airflow issues.

punchline.text: It's not just heat. How air moves through the drum shapes every cup.

quiz.question: What happens when there is insufficient airflow during roasting?
options: Trapped smoke is absorbed by the beans, creating harsh off-flavors

details.summary: Airflow inside the roaster carries heat to the beans and removes chaff and smoke. Increasing airflow during development can brighten acidity by speeding heat transfer, while reducing it retains more body. Mastering airflow is as important as managing gas or heat input.
details.whyItMatters: Airflow is a powerful yet often overlooked lever. Roasters who understand it gain an extra dimension of control beyond temperature alone.
takeaways: Airflow carries heat and removes chaff and smoke from the drum
Higher airflow tends to increase brightness and acidity
Lower airflow retains more body and roast-driven sweetness

faq.question: How does airflow differ between drum and fluid bed roasters?
faq.answer: Drum roasters rely mostly on conduction with supplementary convective airflow. Fluid bed roasters suspend beans entirely on a stream of hot air, making airflow the primary heat transfer method.

faq.question: Can adjusting airflow compensate for too much heat in the drum?
faq.answer: Partially. Increasing airflow can carry away excess heat and slow the rate of rise, but it also changes the flavor profile. It is better to reduce gas input first and use airflow as a complementary adjustment.
